https://www.dw.com/en/spain-will-send-tr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I1Ze Video footage showed large crowds moving round the breakwater Image: Atlas/REUTERS Advertisement Officials in the Spanish territory of Ceuta on the northwestern tip of Africa on Thursday asked the government in Madrid to declare a national emergency and send the army to help secure its border with Morocco . The call came as video footage showed crowds of people trying to walk around the breakwaters separating Moroccan and Spanish territory or otherwise scale the border fence. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged an "immediate response." Spain's Interior Ministry said later on Thursday that its armed forces would send personnel to Ceuta to support the border guards. "The Armed Forces will reinforce the Guardia Civil in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain civil security in the city of Ceuta," the ministry said. What had happened in Ceuta during the day? The Guardia Civil said that crowds broke through the fences into Spain after overwhelming police at the city's breakwater. Video footage showed hundreds swimming across from the Moroccan side, using inflatable inner tubes and other flotation aids. "The situation is absolute chaos," Rachid Sbihi, head of the association that represents Spain's Guardia Civil in Ceuta, told the Associated Press. "It's not possible to give precise numbers but there are thousands of migrants crossing," he said, adding that the border had "totally collapsed." The AFP news agency cited a spokesperson for the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta as saying that nine people had died amid the offshore rush. The scenes were reminiscent of a similar flashpoint at the border crossing in May of 2021 when more than 8,000 people entered the territory in just two days. In recent days, rescue parties had already noted increased numbers of people trying to swim around the border checks. An official from Spain's Guardia Civil policing the border described the situation as 'absolute chaos' Image: Atlas/REUTERS What did the regional government say? Juan Jesus Vivas, head of the Ceuta regional government, called for the Spanish government in Madrid to declare an emergency on grounds of national security, asking for more police and for the army to be deployed on the border. This followed a meeting of the city's board of spokespeople, who reached a unanimous agreement. "Yesterday, I spoke out to warn of the extreme gravity of the migration crisis we are enduring," Vivas wrote online. "Today, mere hours later, the situation is even more critical: another night of mass arrivals, nearly a thousand people waiting outside the CETI [Temporary Migrant Reception Center], our reseources completely overwhelmed, and another life lost at sea." The head of the regional government said its migrant reception center known as CETI had nearly a thousand people waiting outside. Here you see a much smaller crowd outside the facility on Sunday. [FILE: July 26, 2026.] Image: Antonio Sempere/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance He said that the small city was facing "a humanitarian and social emergency" of national proportions. "We cannot face this pressure alone — pressure that has resulted in the arrival of between 1,500 and 2,000 people in just 10 days, equivalent to 2% of our population." He wrote that "with every passing hour, the situation becomes more difficult" in the territory of around 85,000 people. How did Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez respond? Soon after the call for help from Ceuta, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government in Madrid was "fully committed to providing an immediate response" to the situation. "We are mobilizing all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necesssary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible," Sanchez wrote, adding that he had just said as much directly to Vivas. "This is the moment to build solutions, with responsibility and cooperation," he said, not going into specifics in the post. Sanchez's Interior Ministry said that the Moroccan government was "closely cooperating" with Spain to handle the situation and that Moroccan police were stopping "numerous people" trying to cross the border. It said that both countries had agreed to work together "for the return, as soon as possible, of all the people who entered Ceuta illegally." Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska made plans to visit Ceuta on Friday and evaluate the situation, the ministry said. Why is the rush happening now? It's not yet clear why large groups are suddenly seeking entry to Ceuta in the past few days, even though a couple of relatively recent developments at least bear a tangential relationship to the issue. Earlier in July, the Spanish Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not immediately be pushed back across a border in the same way as they could at a land border crossing. The Ceuta and Melilla enclaves in North Africa bordering Morocco do present exceptional cases where this ruling is concerned, in that it is technically possible to enter them "by sea" despite the fact that you are essentially circumventing a border crossing on land, not crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Mediterranean. One less recent development that attracted international attention, meanwhile, is the Spanish government's offer of amnesty and residency permits to migrants who can demonstrate that they had already entered the country without legal authorization. However, that rule only applies to people who can prove they were already in Spain when it came into force, so it does nothing to improve the prospects of staying for people entering by irregular means now. Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, at least, drew a parallel between the amnesty and Thursday's events, calling for the EU's open-border Schengen area to be "closed to Spain," and alleging that the amnesty had encouraged human trafficking. Tajani's Spanish counterpart, Jose Luis Albares, condemned the Italian minister, saying it was "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery." https://www.dw.com/en/hundreds-flee-as-b.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ItqE Massive plumes of smoke began spreading towards Germany, leading authorities to warn residents of potential evacuations Image: Christoph Reichwein/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Belgium is battling its largest wildfire on record which has burned around 2,700 hectares (6,700 acres) in the eastern High Fens nature reserve near the German border. The fire has approached to within 3 kilometers (2 miles) of the German border, causing authorities in Germany to warn of smoke danger. On Saturday, the European Union deployed three helicopters and two water bombers as Belgium deployed additional firefighters in a bid to bring the massive blaze under control . The blaze is described as by officials as the largest in Belgium's modern history Image: Laurent Cavenati/Belga/AFP Authorities ordered around 600 residents in parts of Waimes, Sourbrodt and Buetgenbach to evacuate as shifting winds and heavy smoke raised concerns that the fire could reach homes. Tourists were also advised to leave the area. "You can't see a thing anymore, there's smoke everywhere," David Rodolfs, a restaurant owner in Waimes, told the AFP news agency. A gymnasium in a neighboring municipality was opened up to offer shelter. Reinforcements were pulled from across the country to fight the blaze Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO How have firefighting efforts fared? The blaze, which broke out on Friday, has spread rapidly across peatlands and pine forests. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told AFP he was "shocked" at the fire's speed and extent of the destruction. "There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said. Difficult terrain has hampered firefighting efforts, with operations relying heavily on aerial resources and forcing firefighters to allow difficult-to-access areas to burn, according to Yernaux. Meanwhile, Belgium activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, bringing in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands. Firefighters from Germany and Luxembourg have also joined the response, while farmers have helped emergency crews by wetting down the area. Residents in parts of the nearby villages were ordered to evacuate on Saturday afternoon as a precautionary measure Image: Dimitri Korczak/AFP Residents in Germany's Monschau warned of possible evacuation Authorities in the German town of Monschau in the Eifel region, which is located just 2 kilometers from the border, have warned residents to prepare for possible evacuation. They also warned of health dangers from smoke and have advised people living in three districts of the town to temporarily seek accommodation elsewhere if possible. However, the local fire brigade has said it does not expect the fire to enter German territory any time soon. "We are continuing to monitor the situation," Philipp Krüger, the operations manager of the Monschau fire brigade, told the DPA news agency. Local farmers have headed to the fire zone to support emergency crews Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO Monschau, a major tourist attraction in the Eifel region, has some 12,000 residents. It is particularly known for its picturesque Old Town with its half-timbered houses. It is located just some 23 km from the site of another major blaze in Germany's Eifel region that forced some 2,000 people from their homes on Friday. Climate change making wildfires spread faster Belgium has experienced another spell of extreme heat this week , with temperatures reaching 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country. Scientists say human-caused climate change is increasing the likelihood of hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer. European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib called the blaze the latest sign of the "climate upheaval" affecting the continent. "Never before has the wildfire season started so early in the year and reached such northern latitudes," she said. https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-allies-in-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ODbp Germany's Johann Wadephul, Poland's Radoslaw Sikorski, Norway's Espen Barth Eide and the UK's Ed Miliband shared a stage at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday Image: Dominik Butzmann/photothek.de/picture alliance Advertisement The foreign ministers of Germany , Norway , Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday. This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland , and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap . What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine? German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections. "I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday . "We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said sanctions should continue being imposed on Russia's economy as attacks on Ukraine persist Image: Jörg Blank/dpa/picture alliance UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words. "Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border. Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, meanwhile, said he was counting on "our MAGA president" — a reference to Andrzej Duda of the rival PiS party whom Trump has often praised — to use his "friendship" with Trump to do two things. "Number one: to secure a permanent US base in Poland. And, number two: to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor , and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression, and you end the war by convincing the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," Sikorski said. Norway's Espen Barth Eide said it was important to focus on the actions of the last four years, also welcoming Monday's latest round of Russian sanctions. "I feel that what we've done over the last years ... all of this is a very strong signal that Europe, together with Canada and — on most good days — also with the US, we are sending a very clear message to Putin," Eide said. Facing criticism at home as well, Trump on Tuesday said that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. He also said that other countries would be buying Russian diesel as part of the deal he announced, without being deemed to breach US sanctions, rather than the US buying it itself. This contradicted or possibly corrected his earlier statements. The first two Starlink arrests took place in the small German town of Nürtingen in the southwest, far from Poland's borders Image: Enrique Kaczor/dpa/picture alliance Wadephul: Starlink sabotage shows Europe 'in the crosshairs' of Russia Wadephul also told reporters during his visit that he had spoken with his opposite number Sikorski about the investigations into a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month. Two people with Turkish citizenship were arrested in Germany in the southwestern town of Nürtingen, not far from Stuttgart, on Monday. Based on comments from Polish officials, they are suspected of connections with organized criminality but are thought to have been working on behalf of Russia. Wadephul said that this and other hybrid incidents across the continent showed that "we are in Russia's crosshairs." The satellite-based Starlink internet service is used extensively by Ukraine's military and so the fire was thought to be targeting accessibility across the border in the warzone. "We're being attacked and it's not just happening in Ukraine but all across Europe," Wadephul said. "That means we must strengthen our cooperation." But he also said that the arrests in Germany, which will likely lead to an exatradition process, showed how the security systems were working — both at the policing and intelligence-gathering levels. He said he did not believe Russia would succeed in "dividing us" with such campaigns, saying that instead he expected they would galvanize European allies. A private Polish broadcaster meanwhile reported two further arrests in Germany on Tuesday, although German authorities did not immediately comment on them. Miliband and Sikorski, who spent many of his younger years in the UK, also held a joint press conference in Warsaw on Tuesday Image: Neil Milton/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance Miliband praises Zelenskyy, but says 'let us take seriously' energy ceasefire idea UK Foreign Secretary Miliband praised Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine . However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter. "So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need," Miliband said. Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so. Wadephul added that, if possible, any such efforts to broker a partial ceasefire should also seek to incoporate grain exports and shipments in the Black Sea, particuarly to North Africa. "This is still necessary. And let us please not forget this and urge Russia also to be ready to enlarge the ceasefire, not only for the energy sector but also for the Black Sea. Because this is needed to stop a lot of people in North Africa from falling into hunger," he said. https://www.whec.com/ap-top-news/drones-.text: Drones hit ships in Black Sea, sinking 1 and prompting rescue operations, Bulgaria says By The Associated Press Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev speaks during a handover ceremony of the remains of medieval ruler Czar Samuel, in Thessaloniki, northern Greece, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Giannis Papanikos) SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — Drones struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. The Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship Dignity sank after it was hit by a military strike. Five sailors were rescued, while a search for the other 11 crew members continued, Varna district Gov. Mario Smrkov said. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from the Ukrainian-operated coastal freighter Chelsea 3, sailing under the Maltese flag, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries, Radev said in a video posted to social media. The crew, which included seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijani citizens, reported the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. The strikes on the two ships happened 20 miles and 21 miles (32 and 34 kilometers) from the Bulgarian coast. During an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council on Tuesday, Radev called the attacks “absolutely unacceptable” and said Bulgaria was seeking NATO and European Union assistance. While authorities do not possess clear evidence on who was responsible for the drone attacks, “it makes no sense for Ukraine to destroy its own ships in the Black Sea, and the results of these strikes favor Russia’s interests,” Radev told the Russian Ambassador in Sofia during a meeting on Tuesday, the government’s press office reported. The ambassador said she does not have any information from the Russian defense ministry related to the recent attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea but added that she did not rule out the possibility that “these attacks represent a provocation by a third party.” Radev has said that such attacks are unacceptable and that Bulgaria will continue to investigate the attacks together with its EU and NATO allies to establish the truth. Radev said Bulgaria is suffering significant economic and financial damage and added that his country will initiate talks with neighboring Romania and Turkey on joint proposals to guarantee the safety of shipping in the Black Sea. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha in a post on X on Tuesday blamed Russia for the attacks. “Russia’s latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria’s territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow’s deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea,” Sybiha wrote. “The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponize hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength,” Sybiha wrote. “NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea,” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte wrote on X. He added that NATO had already strengthened its posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting its deterrence and defense posture as needed. The United Nations condemns attacks on civilian ships, especially the most recent ones off the coast of Bulgaria, U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said Tuesday. “It’s very worrisome because these attacks on ships carrying grain, food and other products destined for the global market have multiplied and have expanded recently,” Dujarric said. “It has a terrible knock-on effect on the price of commodities worldwide when you’re also seeing the situation around the Strait of Hormuz, in the Red Sea, not to mention the risk — and also the fatal risk faced by seafarers.” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen “strongly condemned” the drone incidents and said the Black Sea “has become another front of escalation” in Russia’s war in Ukraine. “This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea,” she said in a post on X. “We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable.” European Council President Antonio Costa said in a social media post that the EU stood in full solidarity with Bulgaria following the attacks. He said the growing number of Russian hybrid activities would be discussed at the European Council meeting scheduled for Thursday and Friday in Brussels. The attacks came exactly a week after sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew of a Pulau-flagged vessel. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-13-killed-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OoLM Prefer DW on Google The strike hit a crowded train platform during the morning rush hour Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement At least 13 people were killed and five more injured when a Russian drone struck a passenger train which was stopped at a station in the eastern Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday morning. According to Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia , a jet-powered drone struck a platform on which people were waiting to board a regional train to Zaporizhzhia, about a two-hour journey to the south. "Despite an increased threat warning, people were on the platform," the company said. Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three drones in the daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station. In images circulating on social media, bodies could be seen strewn across a train station platform, with police officers kneeling beside them. Dnipro city mayor Borys Filatov also confirmed the incident, which he called a "tragedy." Zelenskyy issues veiled Trump criticism after 'horrific' attack Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific" and demanded international action from Kyiv's allies. "Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues," he said. "How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating?" he asked, referring to a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin which saw some sanctions on Russia eased in exchange for the release of Russian diesel stocks onto global markets. French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his "deep concern" that Russia continues to "opt for escalation" by targeting civilians. "In this context, we must aim for much more than a localized ceasefire — such as the one recently negotiated for Oleshky ," the French president said on social media, describing Moscow’s rejection of "all proposals to that end" as "intolerable." "Together, we must redouble our efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace and bring Russia to the negotiating table," he said. DW witnesses Ukrainian train evacuation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video How Russia targets Ukrainian trains Russia has been targeting Ukrainian trains and stations since day one of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 , destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing railway workers and passengers. Faced with an increasing number of Russian drone attacks, Ukrainian trains began large-scale passenger evacuations this year — often while trains are already mid-journey. In September alone, more than 5,800 trains had to be evacuated due to the threat of strikes, Ukrzaliznytsia told the AFP news agency. Most evacuations take place in regions near the front line, in the south and east of the country: in Odesa, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia. When a potential Russian strike is detected, the train comes to a halt and passengers are required to leave their carriages and wait at a safe distance until the danger has passed. With commercial air travel in Ukraine shut down due to the war, the country's vast railway network has become essential for transporting people and goods, as well as for entering and leaving Ukraine. Ukraine's unbreakable line: Trains to the frontline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ukraine: More Russian attacks Also on Thursday, authorities reported at least five other fatalities resulting from other Russian attacks across Ukraine. A strike on the city center of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, according to the head of the city's military administration. Elsewhere, a drone slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several — including a six-year-old. https://www.politico.eu/article/inside-u.text: When Vladimir Putin posed for the cameras with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, it marked a rare moment of international acclaim for Russia’s ruler since he ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. By contrast, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will on Thursday find himself among a motley assembly of small and medium-seized countries, convened by two weak European leaders and a rookie without a mandate. The so-called Coalition of the Willing, an alliance of more than 35 nations supporting Kyiv, will gather in Berlin to try to work out how to help Zelenskyy steer his nation through another winter of brutal Russian bombardment and freezing temperatures. Advertisement But some diplomats and officials among Ukraine’s allies worry that this group has suffered a lack of leadership and faltering momentum in recent months, and could be consigned to irrelevance by any deal Trump concocts with Putin. Four European government officials told POLITICO that the political authority of the coalition’s co-chairs — France, Germany and the U.K. — is crucial for Ukraine’s success but also weaker than it has been in years. “The leadership is wobbly in France and Germany,” said one European official, who like others quoted in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “In the U.K., [new prime minister] Andy Burnham seems to be quite solid on Ukraine but he’s still finding his way, so we are waiting.” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz barely clung onto his job this fall after a surge in support for far-right populists led to what he admitted was electoral “disaster” for his center-right Christian Democrats. Emmanuel Macron, the French president, is historically unpopular and faces a wipeout for his centrist allies amid a wave of support for another far-right leader, Marine Le Pen, at next year’s presidential election. Only Burnham has a solid majority backing him in parliament — but he has generally sought to focus on domestic policy since taking over from Keir Starmer in July without winning a general election, and remains relatively untested on the world stage. The crisis coalition The Coalition of the Willing began life on March 2, 2025, a few days after Trump and his vice-president JD Vance unleashed a torrent of criticism at Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, for allegedly not being grateful enough to the U.S. for its support. In the ornate surroundings of Lancaster House in London, which served as a filming location for Netflix series The Crown, Starmer told gathering of 18 leaders he would put British “boots on the ground and planes in the air” if necessary to secure any peace deal that emerged for Ukraine. Macron made similar military commitments. In the year or so that followed, the number of countries in the grouping doubled and Merz formally came aboard as a co-chair of the format. When Trump seemed on the brink of trying to force Ukraine to accept what Europeans regarded as a toxic peace plan a year ago, the coalition became a critical bulwark in Zelenskyy’s defenses, one EU diplomat said. It meant Ukraine’s backers had concrete evidence to show Trump that Europeans were willing to put their own soldiers, equipment and money on the line to guarantee a peace deal. The hope was that this would mean any settlement would be fair. But momentum on peace talks and meetings of the coalition faded and dwindled after the U.S. and Israel launched into a war with Iran in the spring. Thursday’s gathering will be the coalition’s first leaders’ meeting since August. It coincides with the coalition’s first military exercise, held in Poland, where thousands of troops are currently rehearsing how they would maintain any potential peace in Ukraine, despite that prospect still remaining out of reach. Britain’s new kid Burnham is a relative newcomer to the world stage, and was not expected to make foreign policy a central plank of his premiership in the way Starmer did. He confounded that expectation to some extent by holding a flurry of meetings with world leaders upon gaining the keys to No. 10 and reopening a highly fractious debate on the future of the U.K.’s relationship with the EU. Nonetheless, some close observers argue upheaval at the top of government inevitably meant a setback in the highest level of diplomacy. Ed Arnold of the British Foreign Policy Group said “momentum has been lost through a change of PM,” while one U.K. minister noted this was also true for the U.K.’s new defense secretary, Wes Streeting. A British official strongly denied Burnham would have any less energy for the coalition format or for supporting Ukraine than his predecessor. He is “really focused” on sustaining British backing for Ukraine, the official said, pointing to recently announced sanctions and assistance in developing long-range missiles . “The importance of the coalition of the willing is not receding in any way,” the official added. Burnham himself sought to dissolve the distinction between foreign and domestic policy, saying in a speech on Monday : “The world is so interconnected now that it is impossible to disentangle decisions taken in Moscow with what happens on the ground in [his constituency seat] Makerfield.” Trump’s peace drive The revival of the coalition leaders’ engagement comes amid a renewed push from Trump to get a peace deal agreed . The chief objectives of the meeting on Thursday are to develop plans for robust and legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine, including a multinational military force to safeguard a ceasefire; to commit additional funding for Kyiv’s war effort over the next year; to provide military support — especially air defenses against jet-powered drones, and long range strike capabilities; and to coordinate views on the ongoing peace negotiations mediated by Trump’s team. On Wednesday, the European Commission proposed a loan of €45 billion in extra financial support for Ukraine for 2027. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was looking for more contributions from countries outside the EU, adding: “We will discuss the proposal also with our partners in the coalition of the willing.” Another question preoccupying officials and diplomats as they prepared for the Berlin meeting was whether Trump will support Putin’s demands for reshaping European security and NATO’s role on the continent as part of the Ukraine peace process. Many European governments already worry about the U.S. pulling troops out of Europe and some fear Trump’s criticism of NATO members has weakened the alliance’s ability to deter Russian aggression. Yalta fears With these concerns in mind, officials in Brussels and European capitals were keeping a close eye on the meetings between Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, southeastern China. “The danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit [in China] to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force,” said Bronwen Maddox , director of the Chatham House think-tank in London. “Ukraine will be able to hold out, but only with European help.” A German official said the outcome of the Ukraine war is expected to shape Europe’s security architecture for years to come, and this will also form part of the discussion in the group on Thursday. A French official said far from acceding to Putin’s demands, Paris wanted Ukraine to join an expanded NATO. In Kyiv, Zelenskyy’s government is desperate for as much support as possible from its backers, particularly when it comes to F-16 fighter jets, air defenses and money. But the Ukrainians also appreciate that, with the transatlantic alliance now fractured thanks to Trump’s policies over the past two years, an imperfect group such as the Coalition of the Willing is better than nothing and may be as good as it gets. “They are doing a lot for Ukraine in terms of their capabilities,” one senior Ukrainian official told POLITICO. “Burnham is a great guy, he makes a lot of right moves. We are very happy to work with him. Merz and Macron are doing everything they can too. In terms of support Germany is the leader. France is a strong ally.” And the real test of the coalition, the Ukrainian official said, may only come when the war ends and someone has to send troops in to protect the peace. Veronika Melkozerova, Hans von der Burchard, Sérène Nourrisson, Bjarke Smith-Meyer , James Angelos, Victor Jack and Nicholas Vinocur contributed to this report.

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/11/19/vlag.text: Az 1945-ös jaltai konferenciával semmi baj nincs, a ma zajló konfliktusokban pedig el kell fogadni a helyszínen tapasztalható „valós helyzetet” – többek közt ezt mondta Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök a BBC szerint a sajtótájékoztatóján, miután Hszi Csin-ping kínai és Donald Trump amerikai elnökökkel hármasban találkoztak. A másik két elnök eddig nem állt ki a sajtó elé. Putyin kitért az orosz–amerikai kapcsolatokra és arra is, hogy szerinte Kijev és Európa még nem áll készen kompromisszumokra a konfliktus megoldása érdekében. Putyin a Hszivel és Trumppal folytatott találkozóját „a diplomácia történetének fontos fejezeteként” jellemezte, majd azt is mondta, hogy az történelmi jelentőségű volt. Szerinte a „nyugodt és nagyon bensőséges légkörben” zajló tárgyaláson számos kulcsfontosságú kérdésben, ha nem is megállapodásra, de legalább a kölcsönös egyetértésre jutottak. Reményét fejezte ki, hogy folytatják majd a hasonló egyeztetéseket. A három nagyhatalom vezetője az Ázsiai és Csendes-óceáni Gazdasági Együttműködés (APEC) csúcsa alatt egyeztetett csütörtökön a kínai Sencsenben. A megbeszélés másfél órán át tartott , magyar idő szerint 11 órakor ért véget. Az esemény után közös nyilatkozatot is kiadott a három nagyhatalom vezetője, ebben többek közt arról írnak, hogy „a nukleáris háborút nem lehet megnyerni, és soha nem is szabad megvívni”. Az elnök reagált azokra az összehasonlításokra is, amelyek ezt a találkozót a második világháború végén tartott, 1945-ös jaltai konferenciához hasonlítják. Ekkor a Szovjetunió, Nagy-Britannia és az Egyesült Államok vezetői találkoztak. „Mi volt a baj Jaltával? Mi volt benne olyan rossz?” – tette fel a kérdést Putyin. Szerinte Jaltában rögzítették a nácizmus feletti győzelmet. „Nem bánnám – sőt, helyesnek tartanám –, ha a »neonácizmus« feletti győzelmet is rögzítenénk” – fogalmazott. Putyin a jaltai összehasonlításról szólva még azt mondta, hogy az ott kötött megállapodásoknak köszönhető, hogy a világ jelentősebb, globális szintű felfordulások nélkül él. „Igen, sok regionális konfliktus volt, de globális nem. Mi a baj ezzel?” – kérdezte Putyin. Majd kitért azokra a feltételezésekre, melyek szerint a három vezető azért gyűlt össze ma Kínában, hogy „felossza egymás közt a világot”. Szerinte Jaltában senki sem osztotta fel a világot, a konferencia csupán rögzítette a második világháború után kialakult helyzetet. „Ami pedig a mai konfliktusokat illeti, a most fennálló valós helyzetet el kell fogadni” – mondta Putyin, utalva ezzel vélhetően az ukrajnai háborúra. Putyin az orosz–ukrán háborúról amellett, hogy kijelentette, Kijev és Európa „nem áll készen a kompromisszumra”, azt is mondta, bízik benne, hogy Trump valóban az ukrán konfliktus megoldására és az orosz–amerikai kapcsolatok helyreállítására törekszik. A két ország kapcsolatáról még elmondta, hogy azok javíthatók lennének, hozzátette, hogy a Trump-adminisztráció Moszkvával kapcsolatos megközelítése optimizmusra ad okot. Vlagyimir Putyin beszélt a héten az ukránok által harmadik alkalommal támadott , Kercsi-szoros fölött átívelő krími hídról is. Az orosz elnök szerint tárgyalt egy lehetséges tűzszünetről számos, orosz ellenőrzés alatt álló területen, de a híd elleni ismételt támadások után nem került sor tárgyalásokra. „Ezt a hidat nem használjuk katonai felszerelések vagy bármilyen katonai áru, még olaj és olajtermékek szállítására sem” – mondja Putyin. Szerinte a híd „egy egyszerű civil létesítmény”. Hozzátette: válaszolni fognak a támadásokra, a válaszlépések pedig „sokkal fájdalmasabbak lesznek”. Az orosz elnök arról is beszélt, hogy a sencseni csúcstalálkozón az ENSZ reformja, biztonsági kérdések és a nukleáris fegyverek elterjedésének megakadályozása is szóba került. Putyin kijelentette, hogy országának előnye van a nukleáris kérdésben, vezető szerepet tölt be a nukleáris technológia és a nukleáris energia „békés célú felhasználásában”. Putyin a találkozó után azt mondta az őt kikísérő Hszi Csin-pingnek, hogy „köszönöm, hogy megszervezték ezt. Nem hiszem, hogy bárki is számított volna arra, hogy minden ilyen jól fog alakulni.”
